articles.title: GOP defections from Trump start to pile up: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, we round up the latest examples of GOP candidates breaking with President Donald Trump. Plus, Natasha Korecki examines Republicans’ messaging strategy in Texas.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we round up the latest examples of GOP candidates breaking with President Donald Trump. Plus, Natasha Korecki examines Republicans’ messaging strategy in Texas. — Adam Wollner GOP defections from Trump start to pile up By Adam Wollner During his address to the United Nations General Assembly today, President Donald Trump reiterated that he thinks he will be able to strike a deal with Iran to end the war after the November midterms. “I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”Republicans who are on the ballot this fall increasingly would like to see that happen much sooner. Over the past 36 hours, three GOP candidates in competitive races have called for the Iran war to come to an end, tying it to the economic pressure voters are under. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate in Iowa, called yesterday morning for an “immediate end” to the conflict, even though she has voted against several resolutions in the House that would have restricted Trump’s ability to wage the war. Last week, two of her fellow Iowa Republicans, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted for the first time in favor of an Iran war powers resolution ahead of their re-election contests in battleground districts. Several hours later yesterday, former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, released a video on social media saying that “the war with Iran needs to end and end quickly.” And today, another Michigan Republican, gubernatorial candidate John James, said during a news conference that “we need to end this war quickly,” according to The Detroit News. Like Hinson, James, a congressman, has repeatedly voted against the resolutions in the House directing Trump to halt the war. These pivots come amid deepening voter frustration with the war and the state of the economy. According to the new national NBC News poll, 55% of registered voters said they believe Trump’s policies have hurt the economy, and 62% said the military action in Iran has not been worth it. Moreover, 57% of voters said supporting the Iran war would make them less likely to vote for a candidate, compared with 24% who said it would make them more likely. As the midterms near, Republicans are breaking with Trump on more than just the Iran war. As we noted last week, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., released an ad criticizing the president’s deportation agenda. Elsewhere in Florida, Republican candidate for governor Byron Donalds removed most references to Trump on his campaign website. And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, called for an investigation into the business dealings of Donald Trump Jr. (as well as Hunter Biden) following the revelation that a Russian oligarch paid for the president’s son’s post-wedding festivities in the Caribbean. 🎤 Related: Trump’s focus on the press distracts Republicans from pocketbook issues ahead of Election Day, by Peter Nicholas, Yamiche Alcindor, Garrett Haake and Julie Tsirkin Republicans search for a messaging balance in Texas Analysis by Natasha Korecki In interviews, focus groups and polls, there’s little doubt voters’ minds are squarely on the economy these days. It’s no different in Texas, where a pivotal Senate race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico could help determine the balance of power in Congress. But GOP ads in the state have so far focused in large part on an anti-transgender message, an attempt to revitalize the party’s 2024 strategy. In our interviews with Republican strategists over the last week, there was some divide on how much to emphasize transgender issues in the midst of economic strain. One said that spending on trans-related messaging was a waste of money. “If it ain’t about the economy, don’t say it,” said the strategist, who was not authorized to comment publicly on the race. A new NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll bears that out. Among likely Texas voters, 6% said abortion and trans rights ranked as their most important issue. The economy dominated concerns: 47% said either the economy and jobs or inflation and the cost of living were the most influential factors in how they would vote in November, followed by immigration. Still, Texas Republicans are leaning on anti-trans messaging. The Paxton campaign put out a news release today headlined: “Highlighting James Talarico’s Favorite Drag Queen.” Digital ads from Elon Musk’s America PAC have focused on transgender issues. And a super PAC tied to the Senate Leadership Fund launched an ad saying Talarico is “for they/them not you,” in which he is featured saying he is in the fight for transgender kids every day. So why highlight transgender issues when they’re not a top voter concern? Democrats would say it’s pure deflection as President Donald Trump’s approval rating sinks as an unpopular Iran war persists and grocery and gas prices soar. But recall that it was Talarico’s background as a seminarian and his unique ability to talk about God as a Democrat that pushed his national rise. Repeated GOP messaging calling him “woke,” “radical” and “weird” goes toward undermining that image. Our sources also tell us there is so much Republican money flooding in that they can afford to hit Talarico from all sides. For instance, the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which so far announced $15 million in spending, has ads that mention China and taxes. Then there are those Republicans who have a more simple reason. Terry Schilling, who runs the American Principles Project, a conservative group that focuses on social issues, contended its messaging on transgender policies was moving soft Democrats to Paxton, saying: “These issues still work.” That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: The Memo: Ocasio-Cortez fuels speculation about her presidential plans in new interview
articles.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) spurred new and avid speculation about her political intentions on Tuesday, when an extensive interview with her was published in The New York Times. Much of the chatter about AOC, as she is widely known, has centered on the idea that she might seek the presidency. But another route has always…
articles.body:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) spurred new and avid speculation about her political intentions on Tuesday, when an extensive interview with her was published in The New York Times.

Much of the chatter about AOC, as she is widely known, has centered on the idea that she might seek the presidency. But another route has always been available to her given that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is up for reelection in 2028.

The Times story suggested that the Democratic representative was still making up her mind about what lies beyond November’s midterm elections.

Schumer is a legendary political operator first elected to the Senate in 1998.

But his overall approach has engendered criticism from the left, who believe he is not confrontational enough with the Trump administration. Schumer’s age, 75, is also an issue for those who contend Democrats need a new generation at the helm.

Those concerns could open the door to a successful primary challenge from Ocasio-Cortez, almost four decades younger and an icon to many on the left of her party.

She seems in no hurry to close off the option.

The Times journalist to whom Ocasio-Cortez spoke, Shane Goldmacher, noted that her two choices appeared to be a Senate run against Schumer or a White House bid.

“Every element of this is something that’s within consideration,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

The story also noted that Ocasio-Cortez’s Senate calculus could be complicated if Schumer piloted Democrats to a majority in the upper chamber in November.

Such an outcome was once considered at the outer edges of plausibility, given that many of the battleground states usually lean Republican. But a Democratic majority has become more realistic as President Trump’s approval ratings have dropped amid the war on Iran, persistent voter concerns about the cost of living and numerous controversies.

The New York representative noted wryly that a Democratic-majority Senate “would honestly be the best possible problem we could have as a country” and added, “We’re working hard to have that problem, and I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.”

The question of Ocasio-Cortez’s plans is one of the most intriguing within the Democratic Party.

When it comes to the idea of a White House bid, skeptics look askance at the idea of a young, left-wing Latina having a real shot at winning the key swing states upon which presidential elections tend to hinge — places like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Arizona.

But AOC’s boosters have a raft of arguments to make in her favor.

She is by far the best-known and most charismatic figure on the left who could plausibly run for the White House in 2028 — especially given that her political mentor, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), is now 85.

The progressives have momentum in the party right now, as seen in the rise of figures like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Florida Senate nominee Angie Nixon.

Ocasio-Cortez, with her massive social media following and ardent fan base, would also have no problem raising money. On the largest prediction markets, she is either the favorite or second-favorite to become the Democratic nominee.

Some local chapters of the ascendant Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have passed resolutions backing an Ocasio-Cortez presidential bid, even as she has appeared to create some distance for herself from the hardest edges of the left.

In an August interview with ABC’s “This Week,” she approvingly cited a colleague’s declaration that “Woke 1 was crazy.”

The journalist Peter Sterne noted Tuesday that at least one DSA chapter, in southern New Hampshire, has pushed for a run by the more uncompromising Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) instead.

Some on the left have misgivings about Ocasio-Cortez running for higher office despite holding her in high esteem.

Progressive strategist and organizer Jonathan Tasini told this column he thought, if elected, Ocasio-Cortez would “make a terrific president” — in part “because she has the emotional intelligence that is lacking in virtually every other politician I’ve ever interacted with.”

But whether it was a matter of a White House run or a bid for Senate, Tasini questioned how truly successful AOC could be, given that her progressive worldview is shared only by a minority of Democrats in Congress.

“There is virtually no chance in 2028 that she would then have a majority in the House that would share her viewpoint or, in a fantasy world, a Democratic Senate that would be ready to pass ‘Medicare for All.’ So, she sets herself up to be opposed by significant portions of the Democratic leadership, which then sets her up for failure,” Tasini cautioned.

Still, it would clearly take at least one election cycle — and possibly many more — to bolster the progressive presence on Capitol Hill.

Some of Ocasio-Cortez’s comments, including in the new interview with the Times, suggest she thinks that anyone who waits for the perfect moment ends up waiting forever.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she told Goldmacher. “Life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

One of the traits that makes Ocasio-Cortez unusual, by any normal political standards, is a willingness to make public the kinds of thoughts other officeholders keep private.

That was true in an intimate sense this summer, when she offered regular social media updates on her decision to begin the process of freezing her eggs.

But it is also true when it comes to political calculation. To the Times, she mused on the barriers that have traditionally faced female candidates.

“This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” she wondered.

Two intertwined questions — is the country ready for AOC, and what is AOC ready for? — will captivate Democrats for months to come.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

Evelyn Miller, 37, of Emmaus, pleaded guilty Sept. 16, to illegally voting in the election. DHS said Miller registered online on Oct. 9, 2024, less than a month before she voted in person in the Nov. 5 general election. HSI and FBI agents interviewed Miller at her home in July 2025. Miller told investigators she registered online before the election and then went to her polling place in Emmaus to vote on Election Day, according to DHS. SEVEN NONCITIZENS CHARGED IN NORTH TEXAS ELECTION-INTEGRITY INVESTIGATION Miller had received lawful permanent resident status July 19, 2024, during the Biden administration, DHS said. "This alien from the Philippines pleaded guilty to illegally voting in the 2024 election in Pennsylvania," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. "Thanks to the hard work of the men and women of HSI, as well as our partners at the Department of Justice, this alien will soon face justice for her efforts to subvert our elections. American elections are for Americans only." HSI investigated the case with the FBI. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ARRESTED IN INDIANA FOR ALLEGEDLY VOTING IN FEDERAL ELECTION: DHS Miller's case comes as the Justice Department pursues a broader group of election-related cases stemming from the 2024 election. Miller is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 16. She faces up to one year in prison, one year of supervised release and a $100,000 fine, according to federal prosecutors.

articles.title: Hunter Biden responds to GOP senator’s request: ‘I’ll sit next to Don Jr. and testify any time’
articles.summary: Hunter Biden, former President Biden’s son, on Tuesday responded to a request from a GOP senator for both himself and President Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr. to testify before Congress. “Sen. Curtis of Utah has suggested that Don Jr. and I should testify before Congress,” the younger Biden said in a post on the social…
articles.body:
Hunter Biden, former President Biden’s son, on Tuesday responded to a request from a GOP senator for both himself and President Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr. to testify before Congress.

“Sen. Curtis of Utah has suggested that Don Jr. and I should testify before Congress,” the younger Biden said in a post on the social platform X Tuesday. “I say bring it on. I’ve already given more than seven hours of sworn testimony. More than three dozen witnesses testified across two chambers.”

“I had no foreign business dealings while my father was president. None. I painted paintings, and I still do,” he added. “I’ll sit next to Don Jr. and testify any time, any place.”

Republican Sen. John Curtis (Utah) sent a letter to Senate Judiciary Committee leaders requesting they investigate President Trump’s and former President Biden’s business dealings and subpoena their sons to testify in front of Congress.

The Utah senator said that reports on foreign interests using the presidents’ sons for accessibility to their fathers “raise legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president’s family and whether such a relationship can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment.”

Curtis’s push to subpoena Trump Jr. was a political earthquake only a few weeks out from this year’s midterm elections. The Utah senator’s fellow Republicans in the upper chamber have been wary about entering Trump’s crosshairs, especially those running for reelection.

Curtis pointed to Hunter Biden’s “substantial business with foreign entities, including interests in China and Ukraine, while his father held or sought public office” and recent ProPublica reporting that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev shelled out a large portion of the expenses for Trump Jr.’s three-day after-wedding party in the Bahamas.

The Hill has reached out to The Trump Organization for comment.

articles.title: 5 takeaways from Trump’s whirlwind day at UN General Assembly
articles.summary: President Trump threatened the annihilation of Iran if its leaders refuse to strike a deal and framed the U.S. as conquerors of Venezuela, while promoting himself as a problem solver in his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. “To the victor go the spoils,” Trump told the crowd, touting…
articles.body:
President Trump threatened the annihilation of Iran if its leaders refuse to strike a deal and framed the U.S. as conquerors of Venezuela, while promoting himself as a problem solver in his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

“To the victor go the spoils,” Trump told the crowd, touting an oil deal with Venezuela after he launched a military operation removing its authoritarian leader in January.

The president’s remarks at the global summit kicked off a whirlwind day that included a secret meeting between U.S. officials and the Iranian delegation, with the two sides at an impasse nearly seven months into the war.

Trump also signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that ended a standoff over his threats to invade or annex the Arctic island.

Here are five takeaways from Trump’s appearance at the U.N.

U.S. officials met with the Iranian delegation for three hours on Tuesday, Trump told reporters, pointing to his top envoy for negotiations Steve Witkoff. The president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, also attended the meeting.

“I feel very good right now,” Witkoff said, hesitating to answer reporters’ questions about the talks.

Iranian officials have not confirmed whether the meeting took place. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi were in town for the summit.

Earlier, Trump had laid out a stark choice for Tehran in his speech to the U.N. — a deal to give up their nuclear program and reap investments from the U.S., or risk annihilation.

“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness for generations?” Trump posed to the global body and suggested Iran was waiting to see if he is in a weakened position after the midterms in November.

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” he said.

The fallout over Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico loomed heavily over the global summit.

While a major network did not travel with Trump following the White House TV pool’s decision to boycott in solidarity with CNN, the president was pressed on the matter throughout the day.

Trump predicted a federal judge “probably will” rule in the trio’s favor after the three banned media outlets sued the administration on Monday.

“He’s not a particularly fair judge, so you never know,” Trump said, referring to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who the president nominated to the federal bench during his first term.

CNN was originally slated to travel with Trump in the pool. The ban did not stop the network from covering the president at the event in New York and even getting a question in as Trump entered the U.N.

“You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to be covering me,” Trump told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins.

The U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed a new security agreement on Tuesday that would allow Washington to build two new military bases on the Arctic island and ice out Beijing and Moscow from economic investments on the world’s largest island.

The U.S. is now planning to reestablish a military base in south Greenland in Narsarsuaq and another on the eastern side of the island in Mestersvig.

Under the deal, the U.S. would be allowed to build more military bases and “modernize and expand its activities” at the Pituffik Space Base, where about 150 U.S. service members are already stationed.

“You go back way back in the line of presidents, and almost every president at least mentioned it,” Trump said in brief remarks on Tuesday. “But most of them just mentioned it. Some really wanted to make a deal and never got done. But we’re getting it done.”

The deal came after months of tensions, with Trump at one point threatening to use military force to seize Greenland, the semi-autonomous Danish territory.

Trump sought to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” during his remarks to the U.N. General Assembly but largely dismissed concerns about the technology and calls for global cooperation on its regulation.

The president told the body that AI would be referred to as “super intelligence” going forward in U.S. documents.

Trump went on to say using the term “artificial” makes the technology “sound fake.”

“It’s not fake. It’s actually amazing. But we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports,” he said.

“In other words, welcome to the new world of super intelligence — SI,” the president continued. “Let’s see if that goes. It sounds much better. It is much better, and it’s much more accurate.”

Super intelligence is already defined as a form of AI that exceeds human intelligence. It is both the ultimate goal of many frontier AI firms and the greatest worry among those warning about it running rampant.

Trump said he supports a diesel export ban, amid soaring fuel costs linked to the U.S. war with Iran. The conflict has blocked energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea, amid fighting between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels in Yemen.

“I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel,” the president said in response to reporters’ questions and suggested a decision on the ban could happen “fast.”

The president’s remarks underscored the drastic choices facing the administration just weeks before the midterm elections. Republicans are facing increasing odds that they could lose their majorities in the House and Senate related to Trump’s plummeting popularity over the rising cost of living and the war with Iran.

Trump’s approval rating hit an all-time low on Monday, 32 percent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey. Almost two-thirds of Americans say the U.S. is not winning the conflict with Iran, according to a CNN poll released Tuesday.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Voters question whether AI’s promise outweighs its risks
articles.summary: A Fox News survey finds 71% oppose AI data centers in their area, but 52% favor remote locations, revealing a stark NIMBY divide among voters.
articles.body: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly politicized ahead of the midterm elections, the latest Fox News national survey finds voters struggling to reconcile the technology’s promise with the economic and environmental costs of the data centers needed to power it. They are especially against allowing centers in their communities while favoring them in remote locations, creating a "Not In My Backyard" dynamic. A 71% majority opposes building AI data centers in their area, including 46% who strongly oppose them. Both of those numbers are up a touch since earlier this summer. However, the survey reveals a paradox: a 52% majority favors building them in remote locations (44% oppose). FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS The central contrast is seen across community types, as about 7 in 10 urban, suburban and rural voters oppose data centers in their backyards. That consensus fades regarding remote facilities. Half of urban voters (50%) and a majority of suburban voters (57%) favor building them there, while 51% of rural voters remain opposed. Women, White voters, those without a college degree and Democrats are more likely than men, non-White voters, college graduates and Republicans to oppose data centers, whether near their community or elsewhere. When presented with arguments for and against data centers, reactions are nuanced. By roughly 30 points, voters are less likely to support construction if told data centers could strain local water supplies (by 28 points), raise energy bills (29 points) or grow to an enormous size (29 points). FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR Opposition softens when voters see direct benefits to daily life or national interests. They are more likely to be supportive if told data centers are necessary for online activities such as streaming and banking (9 points), critical infrastructure like transportation and water systems (13 points) or to help maintain a competitive edge over countries like China (18 points). These reactions to additional information operate against a backdrop of AI pessimism. Majorities of voters are more likely to see AI as bad rather than good for the U.S. economy (54% bad vs. 36% good), mental health (54-34%), society (56-34%), the environment (60-30%) and jobs (63-29%). The lone exception is day-to-day life, where more voters say AI is a good thing by 4 points (47% good, 43% bad), down from an 11-point spread in November 2025 (50-39%). Overall, AI technology is viewed more negatively than positively by 23 points (37% favorable vs. 60% unfavorable), widening from an 11-point deficit in April and 9 points in July. The underlying demographic patterns mirror those for data centers. Democrats (67% unfavorable), White voters without a college degree (65%), women (64%) and independents (64%) are the most negative. The most favorable views come from non-White men (49% favorable), voters with graduate degrees (49%) and MAGA Republicans (46%). AI & The 2026 Midterms On the generic congressional ballot, the Democratic candidate is ahead of the Republican by 7 points overall. Republicans have a 21-point advantage among voters who support building data centers in their communities, narrowing to 9 points among those allowing construction only in remote areas. Democrats are ahead by at least 19 points among voters who oppose data centers in either location. Voters who view AI favorably back the Republican candidate in their district by 7 points, while those with unfavorable views back the Democrat by 17 points. "In this election, the bottom line is that technology is no longer just a tool. It’s a wedge issue," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "As infrastructure demands force AI into the physical world, campaigns that map tech anxiety onto their voter coalitions will shape the midterm narrative." Voters think Democrats would better handle building AI data centers by a 14-point margin. That lead is especially strong among Black voters (D +51), voters under age 30 (D +35), Hispanic voters (D +29), and independents (D +26). It narrows among White voters (D +5) and rural voters (D +7), while White rural voters are one of the few groups to say Republicans would do better (R +4). Cross-party defections also advantage the Democrats: 15% of Republicans prefer Democrats on data centers, compared with just 4% of Democrats favoring Republicans. A few more things… Three-quarters of voters (76%) favor banning AI in kindergarten through eighth grade classrooms, with some of the strongest preference for the ban among moms (81%). CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Support for banning cellphones in K-12 classrooms is also high: 72% favor the policy and 25% oppose it. In addition, a majority supports prohibiting police departments from using automated license plate readers, such as Flock Safety cameras (57% favor vs. 39% oppose). Age creates the biggest divide. Voters under 30 would ban license plate readers by 28 points, while those 65 and over support them by 7 points. Partisans show unusual agreement on banning the cameras, though by different margins: Democrats by 27 points, independents by 23 points and Republicans by 6 points. Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data.

articles.title: Trump eyes diesel export ban
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Trump considers banning diesel exports The Trump administration is considering a ban on exports of diesel as high prices of the fuel put a crunch on American agriculture and trucking. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson When asked Tuesday whether he was considering a ban on…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is considering a ban on exports of diesel as high prices of the fuel put a crunch on American agriculture and trucking.

When asked Tuesday whether he was considering a ban on diesel exports, as some Republican lawmakers have called for in recent days, President Trump said, “I’ve called for that, too.”

“I’ve said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel.’ We make a lot of diesel,” Trump said during a bilateral meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

“I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it,” he added, then called upon Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to expound on the issue.

“We’re examining that, whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work,” Bessent said.

Over the weekend, several Republicans, particularly those from agriculture-heavy states such as Iowa, expressed support for barring diesel exports as prices hit record levels.

The option divides GOP lawmakers, with members from more oil-producing states dismissing the idea as “a gimmick.”

Welcome to The Hill’s Energy & Environment newsletter, I’m Rachel Frazin — keeping you up to speed on the policies impacting everything from oil and gas to new supply chains.

Did someone forward you this newsletter? Subscribe here.

How policy will affect the energy and environment sectors now and in the future:

As fuel costs rise amid the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars, Americans in the Northeast may have to pay significantly more to heat their homes this winter.

Senate Republicans are clashing over a proposal endorsed by Sen. Chuck Grassley (Iowa) and other farm-state Republicans to embargo the export of diesel to increase supply and lower prices at home, something U.S. leaders last implemented during the 1970s energy crisis.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is launching a drinking water quality study that will for the first time look for traces of abortion pills mifepristone and misoprostol — something anti-abortion activists, attorneys general and lawmakers have been lobbying the agency to do for years.

Diesel hit a fresh record of $6.51 per gallon Monday, but prices in the most expensive state are nearly $2 higher.

articles.title: China AI: Data centres rise from the rolling plains of Inner Mongolia
articles.summary: Potato farmers rub shoulders with rows of gleaming new data centres as Trump and Xi meet to discuss AI safety.
articles.body:
In the expansive grasslands of Inner Mongolia, farmers are picking plump potatoes alongside new neighbours: huge, rectangular blocks that will fuel China's AI platforms.

Ulanqab, with its steppes and volcanoes, is an unlikely digital frontier. For years, it has been China's official "potato capital". But now its fields have also become construction sites for a slew of data centres, as Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping meet to discuss AI safety among other things.

Hundreds of workers in yellow helmets carry heavy equipment into the building site as welding sparks fly off metal scaffolding. Above them huge cranes move with precision to build rooftops, while men balance on ladders to plaster brickwork.

"This is China speed," jokes one worker. "An infrastructure maniac," is how he describes his country, laughing as he walks away. “There is one phase every year. This is the second phase," explains an electrical engineer. "There will be many more phases afterwards."

Artifical intelligence sits at the heart of China's contest with the United States and the key to it is the computing power inside the data centres here.

To the Chinese Communist Party, these buildings are critical for the country's economic and national security. Once finished, they will help drive its mission to embed AI across 90% of industries and society by 2030.

China's not just building the infrastructure. It's also creating a pool of talent: young engineers and researchers who now see their country as a place of opportunity, partly because tensions with the US and Trump's restrictions on immigration have soured the American dream.

"Fewer students and researchers are heading to the US, and more are returning from the US to China. That is very clear," says Jack Zhang from the University of Science and Technology of China.

He himself was recruited by a high-level programme after studying at Yale in the US, and Cambridge in the UK.

"I wanted to take some of the AI work I was doing in the lab and apply it to human health and medicine. That requires more resources, more people and sometimes more government support, which can be difficult to access overseas."

China's expanding AI capabilities are one reason why the US says it doesn't want to hit pause on its AI development, despite stark warnings from inside the industry that the technology was moving too fast.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," President Trump said last week. The CEO of AI firm Anthropic, Dario Amodei, called for keeping the US-led ban on selling advanced chips and equipment to China, while warning that a Chinese lead would "pose grave danger for the US and the world".

This is not what Xi will want to hear when he arrives in Washington on Wednesday. The state-run Global Times, which echoes Beijing, dismissed US fears as part of a "Cold War playbook" to "contain" China's rise.

But China is not just focused on catching up to the US.

It is also touting an alternate model. Xi himself is encouraging Chinese AI firms to develop more affordable, open-source models - which allow people, companies and countries to modify it as they wish.

It also pits Chinese models against those in the US where developers including OpenAI and Anthropic use closed-model approaches, and their design elements are kept a secret.

One reason Beijing is in favour of their approach is that it has worked well for them. By sharing the tech, Chinese AI firms have been able to innovate quickly.

This has helped China overcome one of its biggest challenges: a lack of access to advanced chips, which would help unlock greater computing power.

But Beijing also wants a bigger say in writing the rules that govern AI. Xi has repeatedly called for more regulation and a global framework for others to follow.

With calls for AI safety growing, this week's summit at the White House is especially significant. Can the two sides collaborate on regulating AI? Is any talk of a slowdown even realistic?

It certainly doesn't seem like that in places like Ulanqab, where China's AI ambitions are taking shape.

China is building hundreds of data centres - for Huawei, ByteDance, DeepSeek - in sparsely-populated provinces: Ulanqab, Ningxia and Gansu in the north, Guizhou in the south-west.

It has already built up vast renewable energy capacity - wind and solar - in these regions, land is cheaper and the weather cooler, so there is less demand for water.

This doesn't mean there are no concerns or downsides. China wants most of its data centres to be fuelled by green energy by 2030 - but some of its grid is still fed by coal power. Water supply remains a concern in the arid, dry parts of Inner Mongolia.

Entire villages have been relocated, although it's hard to pin down the number or what compensation residents were offered. It's a topic few people will discuss because it can be dangerous to voice concerns too openly.

"This big data has absolutely nothing to do with ordinary people," says one local, speaking anonymously off camera. "What benefits has it brought us?"

He says few locals had found jobs there. Others told us of fears that their land would be taken and they would no longer be able to farm for a living.

But there are optimists too, such as a man who told us his last name was Zhang, standing alongside potato pickers in a field near the data centres.

“China is now at the forefront of the world," he says, adding that his children have managed to find jobs there.

"It's not like the 1960s, when it was relatively backward. China is doing alright now. Whether in economic development or other areas, it is doing well."

Surveys appear to suggest that there is little opposition to AI or its widespread adoption, compared to so many other countries, but it's hard to evaluate these figures in such a heavily-censored climate.

Beijing has been quite clear that it sees AI as a solution to its ageing workforce, and is rapidly automating manufacturing and production. That is producing anxiety over job losses, which, again, is hard to measure.

But this is also a country that is producing around five million science and tech graduates each year, compared to around half a million in the US.

And as more of them stay in China, they see a growing ecosystem for innovation.

AI developer Dang Ronghao, 27, who works for a leading tech company says Chinese campuses are becoming more open, allowing him to talk to researchers all over the world from his base in Shanghai.

"I've seen research combining AI with nuclear fusion, AI with astrophysics, AI with new materials, and AI with the development of new drugs. I think we are entering a good era."

Even so, some argue that China still rewards conformity over challenge. "It's not as open as I wish," says Professor Liu Jun, Department of Statistics and Data Science at Tsinghua University. He has studied at both Harvard and Stanford.

"I keep encouraging students here to ask more questions, to challenge more, but that's hard to change. I think partly it's culture, partly it's the system."

Far from the labs where Prof Liu and others are wrangling with the AI frontier, many Chinese people are still grappling with more immediate economic troubles: a sluggish economy, rising youth unemployment, low spending and property prices that have plummeted. In rural areas, an ageing population is also a growing concern.

"Big data and all that… pretty good – but it has nothing to do with me," says one farmer in Inner Mongolia, as he trundles on a cart to check on his sheep.

He says he has no use for AI. He hardly even uses the internet.

The screen on his phone is smashed, and wifi comes from a pocket dongle for which he pays just over 40 yuan a month.

"There haven't really been any changes for me. I don't know about the future," he says.

This kind of scepticism can become a challenge for Beijing.

So much is changing here and everywhere else in the country, but it's hard to know how many people are as invested as their leaders in this tech-charged future.

articles.title: Former USPS worker indicted after allegedly dumping 300-plus Utah mail-in ballots without delivering one
articles.summary: Damon Matai Seei allegedly separated over 300 mail-in ballots from other mail at the start of his shift and discarded them within 90 minutes.
articles.body: A former U.S. Postal Service (USPS) worker in Utah was indicted after allegedly setting aside more than 300 mail-in ballots at the start of his shift and dumping them without delivering a single one, Department of Justice (DOJ) officials said on charges related to the case Tuesday. Damon Matai Seei, 34, of Payson, Utah, was indicted by a federal grand jury on Sept. 16, on a charge related to the unlawful secretion, destruction and delay of mail. He was arrested Tuesday and made his initial appearance in federal court in Salt Lake City. Federal prosecutors allege Seei was working as a letter carrier on June 3, when he was entrusted with delivering mail to more than 300 people in Eagle Mountain, Utah, ahead of the state's June 23 primary election. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE The mail included advertisements and hundreds of mail-in ballots that were clearly marked as ballots, according to DOJ officials. Officials said Seei separated the ballots from other mail shortly after beginning his shift, did not deliver any of them and discarded them roughly 90 minutes later. Other mail was also discarded, officials said. Several voters later complained to the Utah County Clerk that they had not received their mail-in ballots, U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak for the District of Utah said Tuesday. POSTAL SERVICE THRUST INTO MAIL-IN BALLOT FIGHT AS TRUMP ORDER GETS TIED UP IN COURT Using county databases, the clerk determined that voter participation was unusually low in the area where the complaints originated, according to Holyoak. It remains unclear whether the affected voters ultimately received replacement ballots or were able to vote. Holyoak said federal officials are continuing to investigate and plan to contact affected voters to determine whether they were able to cast ballots. Seei has told investigators that he did not have a political motive, according to DOJ officials. The investigation remains ongoing. SEVEN NONCITIZENS CHARGED IN NORTH TEXAS ELECTION-INTEGRITY INVESTIGATION "When American voters lawfully cast their vote, they should feel confident that it is counted," said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. "Allegedly throwing away hundreds of ballots is a serious federal crime that undermines the integrity of our elections. Ballot integrity is not a partisan issue." Seei's next court appearance is scheduled for Nov. 30.

articles.title: Beyond killer robots: China's real AI threat to America is already here, experts warn
articles.summary: Experts warn Chinese labs are using "knowledge distillation" and free software to undercut U.S. tech dominance, bypass billions in research and supercharge cognitive warfare.
articles.body: While Americans brace for a futuristic AI war of killer robots and bioweapons, experts warn ahead of President Xi Jinping's U.S. visit this week that Beijing is already actively undermining America's global supremacy through AI without ever firing a shot. Experts who spoke with Fox News Digital outlined a stealthy, three-part playbook, which includes extracting the logic of American models, undercutting U.S. developers with free open-source software and ultimately weaponizing those systems for things like cognitive warfare. They laid out how China bypasses billions of dollars in U.S. research through labs that interrogate cutting-edge American AI and copy its capabilities, while simultaneously flooding the global market with free alternatives. "I think a ‘race’ is the wrong metaphor for this," Leah Siskind, an AI research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital. "I think it's kind of like a multi-front war. And in some places, we're winning, and some places we're losing." XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT While top American tech firms have poured billions into building ultra-expensive, proprietary systems, China has focused heavily on distributing free, open-source models across the globe. Siskind warned that because American tech is costly and the U.S. sector has largely neglected open-source investment, many Fortune 500 companies are making the financial choice to run their operations on Chinese models, unwittingly opening the door to potential CCP censorship, hidden backdoors and, ultimately, global dominance. "How can you compete with something that's free when American tech is very, very expensive?" Siskind said. "How can we ensure that a Chinese open-source model would be truly clean, that it'd be truly free of CCP censorship? We can't be — we just wouldn't know. And that's by design. We wouldn't know what sort of trick backdoors might be implanted and how that could rear its head later on." China expert Gordon Chang warned that Beijing is intentionally using these free models to repeat an economic tactic it previously deployed to corner a different industry. "This is a tactic that China used with solar panels," Chang told Fox News Digital. "Beijing sees that one day it will drive out the American models on cost and availability, and they will then dominate global AI." CHAD WOLF: CONGRESS HAS A CHANCE TO STOP CHINA FROM TURNING YOUR CAR INTO A CHINESE SPYBut to flood the market with free software, Beijing first needs the underlying technology and a way to bypass America's massive lead in computing power. Chang noted that the U.S. possesses a commanding lead in physical infrastructure, boasting over 5,400 data centers compared to China's roughly 450, along with far superior microchips. To work around the staggering hardware and energy costs required to train artificial intelligence from scratch, Siskind warned that Chinese labs are closing the gap through a process known as "knowledge distillation," a method where a smaller model essentially interrogates a larger, smarter American model to copy its logic. "They are able to leapfrog the process by kind of stealing this information," Siskind said, pointing to the Chinese model DeepSeek as a prime example. "This is how they were able to release models like DeepSeek in 2025, which was seismic news because they were able to show that they were really competing with cutting-edge American models and had invested a fraction of the resources." US ADVERSARY TURNS UP THE HEAT ON AMERICA’S AI LEAD WITH AN UNDERESTIMATED EDGE The threat is not theoretical. Just last week, the Department of Homeland Security issued a joint cybersecurity advisory warning that Chinese companies are conducting "industrial-scale knowledge distillation campaigns" to extract proprietary capabilities from U.S. frontier models. Beyond economic undercutting and software theft, the experts also warned Beijing is simultaneously deploying artificial intelligence into physical supply chains and public influence campaigns. Rather than sci-fi "killer robots," Siskind emphasized that China's immediate physical priority is "embodied AI," embedding artificial intelligence into real-world infrastructure like factory automation, commercial drones and autonomous supply chains. Chang warned that AI-enhanced propaganda poses a direct threat to American decision-making and democratic sovereignty. "They're very good at cognitive warfare, and they can enhance their capabilities with artificial intelligence," Chang said. "We do not want our elections determined in China. We do not want our critical national security decisions being made in Beijing. And that's not impossible." CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE As President Xi Jinping arrives in the U.S. this week, the experts who spoke to Fox News Digital said the White House must treat these non-cinematic threats with the same urgency as traditional military posturing. To protect America's remaining edge, Siskind said Washington must tighten chip export loopholes, blacklist foreign labs engaging in deceptive distillation and incentivize U.S. open-source development, emphasizing that "it is very important that the most advanced systems are developed under democracy and represent democratic values, as opposed to authoritarian values." CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN For Chang, the stakes of that technological defense extend far beyond standard economic competition. "Xi Jinping throughout this century has been pushing the Chinese imperial-era notion of Tianxia, or 'all under heaven' that China's rulers have a right to rule the world," Chang warned. "That sounds ludicrous to us, but a Chinese regime powered by AI might actually be able to accomplish that. We certainly do not want our decisions being made in the Chinese capital." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Addressing the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, President Donald Trump reiterated Washington's goal of outpacing China, declaring that U.S. government documents will now refer to AI as "superintelligence." "The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of," Trump told world leaders. "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. And we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else. And we're going to keep it that way."

articles.title: Justice Department indicts former postal worker for tossing out mail-in ballots in Utah
articles.summary: The Justice Department (DOJ) unsealed an indictment Tuesday accusing a former U.S. Postal Service (USPS) employee of throwing out around 300 mail-in ballots in Utah. A federal grand jury indicted 34-year-old Damon Matai Seei, of Payson, Utah, last Wednesday on one count of unlawful secretion, destruction, and delay of mail, according to unsealed court records.…
articles.body:
The Justice Department (DOJ) unsealed an indictment Tuesday accusing a former U.S. Postal Service (USPS) employee of throwing out around 300 mail-in ballots in Utah.

A federal grand jury indicted 34-year-old Damon Matai Seei, of Payson, Utah, last Wednesday on one count of unlawful secretion, destruction, and delay of mail, according to unsealed court records. The DOJ accused Seei of throwing the ballots, en route to Utah voters ahead of its June primaries, into a large dumpster.

The former USPS employee was arrested and arraigned at the Orrin G. Hatch U.S. Courtroom Tuesday afternoon.

“When American voters lawfully cast their vote, they should feel confident that it is counted,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a DOJ statement . “Allegedly throwing away hundreds of ballots is a serious federal crime that undermines the integrity of our elections. Ballot integrity is not a partisan issue.”

Seei worked as a letter carrier for the USPS earlier this year, the DOJ said. On June 3, he was delivering mail, advertisements or mail-in ballots to at least 300 Eagle Mountain, Utah, residents. The ballots were being mailed ahead of the June 23 primary election.

The department accused Seei of throwing the mail into a church parking lot dumpster, according to a detention memo . DOJ officials alleged that, in an interview, Seei said he threw out the mail “to lighten his workload,” so he could “presumably” return home sooner.

“Because of Seei’s actions, those voters never received these ballots, and some of these voters were not able to vote in the election,” the DOJ stated.

Prosecutors said they seek to have Seei be released under several conditions, including that he must report to an assigned pretrial officer, maintain employment or seek employment, surrender his passport and not interfere with mail delivery, “especially, the delivery of mail-in ballots.”

The incident comes as fewer voters say they expect to vote by mail and more plan to cast their ballots in person. An NBC News poll released Sunday showed that 36 percent of registered Democratic voters plan to cast their ballots in person at an early voting site, while another 36 percent said they will vote in person on Election Day.

Independents, at 28 percent, said they will vote early and in person, and 37 percent said they will vote on Election Day. Twenty-six percent of Republicans said they will participate in in-person early voting and 53 percent said they will vote in November.

Pollsters said that President Trump’s unfounded claims that mail-in voting encourages election fraud and rigged results, as well as his attacks on the country’s mail-in ballot system, have led some to rethink casting their midterm votes using the method.

articles.body:
MAHA activists call out Trump, RFK Jr. on mRNA

Make America Healthy Again activists, alongside conservatives in the medical freedom movement, slammed President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for failing “to take decisive action” on removing messenger RNA vaccines from the market.

In a strongly worded open letter , the activists threatened to withdraw their political support “if we continue to see inaction.”

The letter speaks to the competing factions within Kennedy’s MAHA movement, which formalized from the political alliance between Kennedy and President Trump. It has elevated issues such as vaccine safety, corporate interests in federal agencies and the presence of chemical additives and pesticides in the food supply.

“We did not fight to place you in positions of leadership so that our clearly stated policy goals would suffer a ‘bait and switch’ that rebranded the grassroots powerful objection to the mRNA platform as a concern about coloring agents in Skittles, ” they wrote.

MAHA helped give Trump an important ally in Kennedy, a longtime Democrat before he endorsed Trump and joined his administration. And Kennedy gave Trump and Republicans access to a new group of voters, which could be key to helping lift the party in a year where Trump’s ratings are underwater.

The letter was signed by more than 100 people, including vaccine skeptics like Robert Malone, a MAHA activist and former member of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s vaccine advisory panel, as well as Mary Talley Bowden, a doctor who leads Americans for Health Freedom.

Other signatories include prominent conservatives and former Trump allies Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), former Rep. Majorie Taylor Green (R-Ga.), political commentator Tucker Carlson, and Peter McCullough, a former cardiologist and Kennedy ally who has been criticized for spreading COVID misinformation.

The signees criticized the recent appointment of Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, who said in her June Senate confirmation hearing that “ mRNA technology is safe and effective.”

They also called out Kennedy’s HHS for approving an mRNA-based flu vaccine, as well as entering into contracts with Pfizer worth more than $1 billion for future mRNA vaccines.

“Neither Republicans nor Democrats could have prevailed” without the MAHA/health freedom vote, the letter stated. “Health freedom voters can and will walk away if we continue to see inaction—or condescending non-policy— on our core issues.”

articles.title: Michigan attorney general Nessel endorses El-Sayed after previous criticism
articles.summary: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel (D) has endorsed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D), weeks after she criticized the Democratic nominee for his response to a March attack on a synagogue in their state. “We have one candidate that I know is going to fight against the Trump administration, is going to fight to protect…
articles.body:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel (D) has endorsed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D), weeks after she criticized the Democratic nominee for his response to a March attack on a synagogue in their state.

“We have one candidate that I know is going to fight against the Trump administration, is going to fight to protect … our physical security, our safety, our health and our futures,” Nessel said alongside El-Sayed on Tuesday’s episode of “For the Sake of the Argument with Lori Goldman.”

The Michigan attorney general blasted El-Sayed’s opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) as someone who “only cares about self-enrichment.”

Nessel backed Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) over El-Sayed in the primary . The state attorney general, who is Jewish , also did not attend the state party’s convention in late August, citing fears of being harassed for her support of Israel.

Last month, Nessel told The Atlantic that El-Sayed made “excuses” for the man who launched an attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township, Mich.

Earlier this year, El-Sayed said the man, who had four members of his family killed in an Israeli airstrike in early March, acted because “hurt people do hurt people.”

But in endorsing El-Sayed, Nessel said there is “no choice” between El-Sayed and Rogers. The Democratic nominee also said he was “grateful” for the state attorney general’s support.

“I’m grateful for your support … and I’m particularly grateful for it because I know we haven’t always agreed on everything, right? And I know we won’t always agree on everything,” added El-Sayed, who has called for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel.

“I know that you care about my kids and have fought for them. And I know you know that I care about your kids and have fought for them and will fight for them. … And that’s the thing that we can do together,” he said, before shaking Nessel’s hand.

As of Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ gives El-Sayed a 68 percent chance to defeat Rogers. The two are battling to succeed outgoing Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

articles.title: Virginia school district faces probe over 9/11 teaching guide telling teachers not to ‘center the extremists’
articles.summary: America First Legal launched a FOIA investigation into Fairfax County Public Schools' 9/11 guidance that tells teachers not to center extremists.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: America First Legal (AFL) has launched an investigation into Fairfax County Public Schools (FCPS) in Virginia after Fox News Digital first exposed controversial guidance for teaching the 9/11 terrorist attacks, seeking to determine who was responsible for developing instructions that tell teachers not to "center the extremists or the acts of the extremists." The conservative legal group announced the investigation after Fox News Digital first reported on the FCPS guide ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks. The district's guidance tells teachers not to "associate the 9/11 attacks with Islam or Muslims" or "center the extremists or the acts of the extremists." LIBERAL VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT: DON'T LINK 9/11 TERROR ATTACKS TO 'ISLAM or MUSLIMS' "We wanna know where this comes from. We wanna know who the school is working with to develop these guidances," America First Legal senior counsel Ian Prior told Fox News Digital. Prior said AFL is seeking to examine how FCPS arrived at the guidance and whether any outside organizations participated in its development, but acknowledged AFL has not yet determined whether that occurred. "We're still seeking to determine how far this goes," Prior said. "That's why we're investigating so that we can get to the bottom of it." The investigation was directly prompted by Fox News Digital's reporting, Prior said. CBC RELEASES POLICY CHANGE AFTER CONTROVERSY ABOUT REFUSING TO REFER TO 9/11 AS ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’ "The reason why we're investigating now is because this was just reported," he said, adding that AFL saw the report "just like everybody else" and wanted to determine who FCPS was working with when the guidance was developed. In announcing its investigation, AFL is accusing the school district of attempting to "sanitize history" and calling for "full transparency regarding who is responsible" for the guidance. The group's announcement directs readers to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request, though the two-page release itself does not detail the records sought. The six-page FCPS guide, titled "25th Anniversary and Commemoration of 9/11," was published Aug. 27 and edited Aug. 31. It directs teachers who choose to commemorate the attacks to carefully follow the district's guidance and use only instructional resources available through the district's Atlas site. FCPS tells educators that lessons about the attacks can unintentionally stigmatize Muslim and Middle Eastern students and instructs teachers to prepare for anti-Muslim rhetoric, create "safe spaces" for Muslim and Middle Eastern students and challenge expressions of bias. A GENERATION CANNOT REMEMBER 9/11. WE HAVE A DUTY TO MAKE SURE THEY LEARN Fairfax County Public Schools did not directly answer Fox News Digital's questions about who authored and approved the guidance, whether outside organizations were involved in its development or whether the district has made or considered changes to the document. The district referred Fox News Digital to a statement published on Sept. 11. In that statement, Superintendent Michelle Reid said FCPS "unequivocally condemn[s]" the 9/11 terrorist attacks and emphasized the district's connection to the Pentagon, military families, first responders and survivors. The statement also said FCPS was "reviewing our materials" in response to community feedback, while maintaining that "the actions of terrorists should not define the entirety of any faith, culture, or community." FCPS's Sept. 11 statement provides some information about how the materials were reviewed, but does not identify who authored the six-page guide or who approved its final language. Prior argued that schools can teach students about the ideology that motivated the Sept. 11 terrorists without assigning collective responsibility to Muslims. BROOKLYN TEACHERS WHO WITNESSED 9/11 AS CHILDREN REVEAL WHAT THEY WANT THE NEXT GENERATION TO REMEMBER The district's guidance similarly states that teachers should make clear that al Qaeda carried out the attacks, while drawing a distinction between the terrorist organization and Muslims as a whole. "When discussing this topic with students, please make clear that the September 11 attacks were carried out by Al-Qaeda, a terrorist extremist organization," the guide states. "Al-Qaeda’s ideology and actions should not be attributed to Islam or to Muslims as a religious community." The dispute centers in part on how much emphasis teachers should place on the terrorists and their ideology when commemorating the attacks. FCPS tells teachers that "the commemoration of 9/11 focuses on those whose lives were lost and those who sacrificed to help others — not those who attacked the United States." The guide encourages teachers to emphasize stories of "resilience, support, and resistance" and use age-appropriate details about the violence. CBC CAVES ON 9/11 ‘TERRORISM’ GUIDANCE AS US, CANADIAN OFFICIALS UNLEASH CROSS-BORDER BACKLASH For elementary students, the district suggests teachers could open by saying, "Twenty-five years ago today, there was an attack on the United States," before allowing students' questions to determine what additional information is shared at the teacher's professional discretion. Its suggested language for older students is considerably more specific, stating that "members of the extremist group al-Qaeda hijacked four planes in a coordinated terrorist attack on the United States" before recounting the 2,977 people killed, including civilians, military personnel at the Pentagon and emergency workers. The guidance also highlights the passengers and crew of Flight 93 who fought back against the hijackers. FCPS said in the guide that its approach reflects the varied experiences of families in the Northern Virginia district, where some were personally affected by the attacks and the ensuing War on Terror. "Many families of military personnel and first responders experienced loss and hardship," the document states, while also saying Muslim families worry about harassment and hate crimes surrounding the anniversary. AFL argues the district's approach goes too far. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Fairfax County Public Schools is attempting to sanitize history and erase the radical Islamic terrorism that struck our nation on September 11, 2001," AFL counsel Will Scolinos said in announcing the investigation. "Parents and the public must have full transparency regarding who is responsible for stripping truth from our children’s classrooms." Prior said AFL has not determined what action could ultimately follow its investigation and that the group's next steps will depend on what it finds. Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani contributed to this reporting.

articles.title: Lawmakers across Americas urge US to end drug boat strike campaign
articles.summary: {beacon} Defense &National Security Defense &National Security The Big Story Lawmakers across Americas urge US to end drug boat strike campaign More than 70 lawmakers from North and South America, including the U.S., Canada and Colombia, are calling on the Trump administration to end its deadly strike campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the…
articles.body:
Lawmakers across Americas urge US to end drug boat strike campaign

More than 70 lawmakers from North and South America, including the U.S., Canada and Colombia, are calling on the Trump administration to end its deadly strike campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific — labeling them extrajudicial killings at sea.

“The rights to life, due process and protections against the arbitrary use of force are core principles of democratic rule of law that our countries have committed to uphold. Allegations of drug trafficking , however serious, do not circumvent or override these protections, nor do they justify lethal force against people who pose no imminent threat,” lawmakers wrote in a 2-page statement Tuesday.

Since early September of last year, the U.S. military has carried out deadly strikes against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, killing more than 220 “narco-terrorists” — actions human rights activists and legal experts have argued are violations of international law .

Trump administration officials have said the deadly strikes are part of the efforts to curb the flow of illicit drugs and dismantle “narco-terrorist” networks in the Western Hemisphere. U.S. officials have not offered evidence that the fast boats are carrying drugs.

The U.S. military has conducted a minimum of 70 strikes on both sides of the South American continent and killed 234 “narco-terrorists” since the campaign began on Sept. 2, 2025.

“We are also deeply concerned that these harmful, illegal operations may be facilitated through other governments’ intelligence sharing, access to military bases and facilities, logistical support and other forms of cooperation,” lawmakers wrote. “Under international law, states may incur responsibility when they provide aid or assistance in the commission of internationally wrongful acts, with a view to facilitating such acts.”

The White House did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

A top U.N. human rights expert Ben Saul said Monday that the lethal boat strikes violate international law and could constitute “ crimes against humanity .”

“There is no right to use force in self-defence against the criminal groups listed as terrorist organizations. Firstly, even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” Saul wrote in the 11-page paper .

In recent weeks, U.S. forces in the U.S. Southern Command theater have also set their sights on another target in the Eastern Pacific, larger fishing boats they have claimed are “floating refueling stations,” The Hill reported .

Instead of blowing up these larger boats with people still on board, the U.S. military will hover a helicopter over the water and have Marines board the repurposed fishing vessels to remove the crew before launching a strike .

“Addressing drug trafficking and transnational organized crime requires effective international cooperation, but that cooperation must be grounded in international law ; respect for human rights and national sovereignty; accountability and transparency; diligent investigative, prosecutorial, and judicial work; a commitment to address corruption; and democratic oversight of security policies,” lawmakers said in Tuesday’s statement.
